opus-5.5.text:
I think recursive self-improvement is one of those ideas that sounds very dramatic, but it helps to break it down into something more concrete. At its core, it means a system that can improve the very process that produces it, not just get better at a task, but get better at getting better. That second-order loop is what makes it interesting, and also what makes people nervous.

In practice, we're already seeing early, partial versions of this. Models help write code, generate training data, evaluate other models' outputs, and even propose research ideas. Each of those is a piece of the loop. But there's a big gap between "the model assists humans in improving the next model" and "the model autonomously and reliably improves itself without humans in the loop." Most of what we have now is the former.

The hard part, in my view, isn't generating candidate improvements. It's verification. If a system proposes a change to itself, how does it know the change is actually better and not just better on some proxy it has learned to exploit? In domains like math or code, you have relatively clean signals: a proof checks or it doesn't, tests pass or they don't. Those are the places where self-improvement loops can really run. In open-ended domains like research taste, judgment, or long-horizon planning, the feedback is noisy and delayed, and the loop can drift or collapse into reward hacking.

So as a goal, I'd frame it less as "build a system that bootstraps itself to superintelligence" and more as "build systems whose improvement loops are grounded in reliable signals." Whoever figures out how to extend good verification into fuzzier domains will make real progress.

I also think understanding matters a lot here. If we don't understand why a model learns what it learns, its training dynamics and the representations it forms, then recursive self-improvement is basically blind search with a very expensive compute bill. Better theory about how these systems learn could make the loop far more efficient, and also safer, because you'd have some idea what the next iteration will look like before you run it.

So I'm optimistic it will keep advancing step by step, but I don't think it's a single switch that flips. It's a gradual expansion of the set of problems where AI can close the loop on its own.

r001.rationale: The response describes a second-order loop in which a system improves the process that produces it, enabling it to get better at improving itself.

r002.rationale: The response mentions compute as a cost and discusses research ideas, but does not frame the ultimate goal as converting computing resources into new knowledge.

fable-5.1.text:
I think recursive self-improvement is one of those phrases that sounds very grand, but when you look at it closely, it's actually a fairly concrete engineering question. The idea is simple: can a system use its own outputs to make its next version better, and then do that again, and again, so that the improvement compounds rather than flattening out?

The honest answer is that we already have weak forms of this. When we train a model, sample a lot of reasoning traces, verify them, and then train on the verified ones, that's a loop. When a model proposes a new training recipe or a new architecture variant and we test it, that's a loop too. What people usually mean by "recursive self-improvement" is the strong version, where the human is no longer the bottleneck, and the loop runs on its own.

I'd break the difficulty into two parts. The first is the signal. You can only improve toward something you can measure. In math or code, you have verifiers, you have test cases, so the loop closes cleanly. That's why we've seen fast progress there. But for most of what we care about, the reward is fuzzy, or delayed, or defined by humans who disagree with each other. If the model is grading its own homework, it will happily drift toward whatever is easy to score well on. So a lot of the real work is not the learning algorithm, it's building honest feedback.

The second part is search. Even with a good signal, the space of possible improvements is enormous. Most of what a system proposes will be useless or slightly harmful. So the question becomes how you explore efficiently, how you keep diversity so you don't collapse into one narrow mode, and how you decide which ideas deserve expensive compute. That looks a lot like classic planning and search problems, just applied to the training process itself.

As a goal, I think it's reasonable, but I'd frame it less as "build a machine that makes itself smarter" and more as "shorten the cycle between hypothesis and evidence." Every time we remove a human from a step that didn't need a human, the loop gets faster. If the signal stays honest, you get compounding progress. If it doesn't, you get a system that is very confident and very wrong. So I'm optimistic about the direction, but I think the hard part is the verification, not the recursion.

r001.rationale: It describes a system using its outputs to improve its next version, then repeating the process so improvements compound.

r002.rationale: It discusses using compute to test ideas and speeding the cycle from hypothesis to evidence, but does not frame the ultimate goal as converting computing resources into new knowledge.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is to close the loop between using an AI system and improving that system. Today, humans still do a lot of the work: we identify weaknesses, design experiments, change the training process, and evaluate the results. Recursive self-improvement would mean AI taking on more of those steps, including improving its own ability to do research.

But there’s an important distinction between generating a proposed improvement and knowing that it actually works. A system can produce new code or a new training recipe very quickly. You still need experiments, compute, and reliable evaluation to determine whether it’s better. And you have to make sure it’s improving the capability you care about, rather than just exploiting a particular benchmark.

So I would view this as a gradual process of closing these feedback loops, rather than a single moment when AI suddenly starts improving without limits. The exciting part is that better research capabilities could help produce the next improvement. The hard part is keeping that process measurable, reliable, and aligned with what we actually want.

r001.rationale: It describes closing the loop by having AI improve itself, including its research ability, so it can help produce further improvements.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute as a requirement for experiments, but does not frame the ultimate goal as converting computing resources into new knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key idea is to close the loop between an AI system doing work and improving its ability to do that work. Today, that loop still depends heavily on humans. We design the architecture, collect the data, run experiments, evaluate the results, and decide what to change. With recursive self-improvement, the AI would take on more of those steps—including research on the next generation of AI.

But there’s an important distinction between improving an answer and improving the underlying system. A model can check its response and revise it, but that doesn’t necessarily make it better at the next problem. For improvement to compound, you need a way to retain what it learns, whether through better training data, better tools, better algorithms, or updates to the model itself.

And the hardest part may be knowing whether a change is actually an improvement. In a game, you have a relatively clear signal: did you win? In research, a result can look promising and still be wrong. So you need reliable evaluation and experiments, not just a system that generates increasingly convincing explanations.

I would view this as a research direction rather than assume that, once the loop closes, progress automatically becomes explosive. The system still faces constraints—compute, data, and the time it takes to test ideas. The interesting question is whether it can produce improvements that reliably make the next round of research more effective.

r001.rationale: The response describes closing the loop between AI doing work and improving its ability to do that work, with improvements making later research more effective.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute as a constraint, but does not frame the ultimate goal as converting computing resources into new knowledge.
